utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Pupovac. Let me take this opportunity once again to remind you that at the beginning of your testimony, you undertook to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. You are still bound by that declaration, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good. And I think we were at the stage where I'm supposed to ask you questions, if I can just sort of find my questions. Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am, yesterday, you said that the Croats shelled their own village. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the extent of the destruction of the buildings as a result of that shelling?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, when a shell hits a wall, it makes a hole and since the buildings are made of stone or brick, depending on which place is hit, this determines the level of damage, because Dalmatian stone is very hard and damage may be lower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe if we can call for that exhibit that shows the damaged buildings so that you can have a look at them and tell us whether they were in that condition on that day. What exhibit is that, Mr. Black? 272? If we can have Exhibit 272 on the screen, please. I'll try and find the page right now, unless Mr. Black can help me on the page, the relevant pages that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can you look at page -- it's page 2, it's 7799. Do you have that on your screen, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I do have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see it's just rubble there. Is that what happened on that day? Was that the extent of the destruction on that day?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This didn't look like that when the army passed through. That place, I never saw such cases. This is just a heap of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of rubble. Go to the next page 7800. Did the houses look like that after the destruction or the shelling?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were they worse than that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Didn't see such cases. This is enormous destruction but there were no such damage inflicted when the army passed through there on the 18th and the 19th, when I was there as well. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you there on the 19th as well?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th and the 19th, the 19th was continuation of the operation towards Nadin so the Territorial Defence was there on the 19th as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Would I then take it that what appears on the next page, 7801, is -- was also not the case? If you can look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask, did I understand it correctly, you were there in Skabrnja on the 18th -- you were there in Skabrnja on the 18th and the 19th of November? Or only on the 18th in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived to the centre of the village of Skabrnja on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: How long have you personally, you, Witness, been there in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there in Skabrnja on the 18th and the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Are you able to describe in words the extent of the damage that you observed on the 18th and the 19th of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were holes, if I can describe it, a hole -- I must describe this with my hands. A hole made by a shell hitting the wall leaving the rest of the building intact but this is wholesale destruction. This wasn't like this when I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now, you also testified that the bell tower of the church was targeted. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What kind of weapon was used to fire at the bell tower?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fire was opened at the bell tower because there was a light machine-gun in the belfry, and fire was opened from the side of the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hear my question. My question is, what type of weapon was used by the JNA to fire at the bell tower? You have told us what was at the bell tower but just what type was used to fire at it?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a tank and an APC, and infantry weapons. I don't know what was used to hit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it should have been either of those three? Either a tank or an APC or an infantry weapon?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You also testified, ma'am, about pulling a young man, a wounded young man, out, a man named Ivica, remember?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ivica was wounded on the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know his last name?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know how he was injured?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wounded in the leg. I can't remember after so many years which leg. I dressed his wounds. He was then transported to the medical centre in Benkovac, first to Smiljcic, to be provided medical assistance by a physician and then later on to Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to other people who were with him when he was injured?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he was wounded, at which place he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that civilians were intermingled with combatants. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you said the reason you knew this was that you saw ten civilians coming out of a cellar from which shots were fired, and that those civilians were then directed by the JNA towards another location where they would be safe. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone remained in that particular cellar?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether any civilians. I know that fire was open from that cellar. I don't know whether somebody stayed behind or whether they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How, then, was it determined that these people leaving the cellar were civilians?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore civilian clothes, without any weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How was it determined who was doing the shooting from the cellar?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can hear shots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was fired at while I was directing people away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Hearing shots will help you determine that shots are being fired. My question is: How was it determined who, between the combatants and the civilians in the cellar, was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Whoever holds a rifle is a combatant. In my opinion, whether wearing a uniform or civilian clothes, if they kill a man, they are a combatant. They are not a civilian as long as they shoot at others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you see people who were having weapons who were in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see. I did not enter the cellars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you also testified about a man called Tomislav Curkovic at whose wedding, shots - AK 47 - were fired. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What ethnic classification is he?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an honest Croatian family. The father of the family did not like what he saw happening at the wedding reception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand that last sentence. What do you mean the father of the family did not like what he saw happening at the wedding reception, the father of Curkovic family.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tomislav's father always shied from conflicts, had very good relations with his Serb neighbours. That is located between our Serb hamlet and the Croatian houses and Croats inhabited all houses until my home. He, father of the family, did not like seeing shots being fired at the wedding reception. He wanted a proper wedding for his son. He lived a long time abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know why these AK 47s were being fired at his home, at this wedding?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they opened fire, but the same one - group - 30 minutes afterwards blockaded the road towards Benkovac. I personally, with three relatives, could not pass that point because I was held at gun point by the young men who were at the wedding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did I get it right that you said that the people who were firing these AK 47s were members of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know all of them. We were a large village and everybody knows everybody else. I can list you households by their family name even now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Later on, you told us about another Curkovic was with a certain Siva [phoen] and they said they were "redarstvenici," members of the MUP. I would imagine then that second Curkovic is also a Croat.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Curkovic, Ivica is a Croat and he was among the redarstvenici or MUP policemen, and the other person, also a member of the MUP, is Sisgora S-i-s-g-o-r-a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sisgora. Now, if I may just go back to the wedding, you wouldn't characterise that shooting that took place there as an interethnic shooting, would you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been [as interpreted] interethnic because there was only one Serb, the best man of Sime Curkovic, attending that wedding reception, no others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But no aim was taken at that best man, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Son-in-law, not best man.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The pretext was that they barricaded the road. They've demonstrated that they were armed. And this is when we saw that they were armed, when, after 30 minutes from the beginning of the reception, they blockaded the road, the young men attending the wedding ceremony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but the shooting was done by Croats. The wedding was a Croat wedding. It couldn't have been interethnic, could it?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not shoot at Serbs then. They wanted to prove their power, their might, that they were armed. I did not say that they were aiming at anybody, but when the barricade was set on the road, they held me at gun point. The round was in the barrel because later on they shot it in the air. I just had to go back from where I had come and I wasn't hurt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's just clarify an answer you gave a little earlier. Did you say it could have been interethnic or did you say it could not have been interethnic?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Couldn't have been on that wedding reception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then -- thank you so much. I understood you better.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barricade on the road was for interethnic purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you a question at some stage and asked you whether you were a member of the JNA at the time, and I think the time was around 1991. Do you remember that question? You don't? Okay.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me remind you how you answered it. You said, "No, not at the time." That's how you answered it. That was at page 70, line 11, on the first day of your testimony. Now, I'm not able to tell exactly what the page would have been -- would be today now that it has changed.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I was never sent -- I was never -- never received from the JNA call-up papers. I was called up by the Territorial Defence of Benkovac and I was under their command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's really what I wanted to establish. You never became a member of the JNA, to this day?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not of the JNA but the TO of the municipality of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand TO. I want to be clear that you never became a member of the JNA or you were one -- you at some stage became a member. The reason I'm asking you this question is because your answer said, "No, not at the time." So you never became a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To this day?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was under the command of theirs when I was in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is 10339, line 24, just for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. On the 18th -- and you may have been asked this question by the Prosecutor but I just want to be sure that it is asked in case it was not. On the 18th of November 1991, did the JNA suffer any casualties apart from Lieutenant Stefanovic and the soldier on the APC?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Skabrnja, there were two killed, and a number of wounded. I cannot specify the number. I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The people killed were two only? Lieutenant Stefanovic and the soldier on the APC?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stefanovic and a Muslim soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said also on that point that the JNA soldiers took cover behind some walls. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What walls were these that they took behind cover -- behind which they took cover.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Dalmatia we have stone dry walls while I lived there. Along the road, each house, each garden, was walled in and it was the safest place to take cover, behind such a wall, not to get hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say that members of the JNA took cover behind garden walls, to homes?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind walls but alongside the road, and people who are in APCs, they remained there, or in a tank, and in Skabrnja there was one tank, one APC, and they were hit by rocket-propelled grenades. These walls run next to the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. And I want to understand clearly what your testimony is. Is it your testimony, then, that the JNA soldiers, those who got off the APCs and the tanks, went and hid behind the walls of the gardens of the homes? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them were courtyard walls. Some are -- some were gardens, Dalmatian villages are not as densely populated as some others. There were gardens or open space between houses, but that region was not that densely populated. There were not many houses there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. I understand. I understand that. What I do want to know is, these walls that you referred to are garden walls along the road?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And these soldiers were taking cover from fire that was coming out of the homes, the very homes, of these gardens?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us what kind of protection the garden walls provided for these JNA soldiers? In other words, did they not fall when they were hit by rocket propellers -- rocket-propelled bombs?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fortunately, it did not hit them, it hit the tank. The tank was hit. APC was not. There were wounded people in Skabrnja, on both sides. I'm not saying that there were only wounded on the side of the Yugoslav People's Army. There were wounded people on the Croatian side as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is mainly focused on the walls at this point in time. Do I understand you to be saying that there was no firing directed at the soldiers who were taking cover behind the walls?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fire. There was gunfire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what became of the walls?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since fire was being opened out of cellars, from infantry weapons, we took cover behind walls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is, as these walls were being fired at, what became of them?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bullets ricocheted off the wall, and that's what happened when the bullets impacted on the other side of the wall, because the walls were made out of hard rock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the walls didn't come down; that's the short answer?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They couldn't have come down if only hit by infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Do you have an imagination, could we go to that photo document, page 7 and page 8? I just browsed through the whole booklet and these two and actually also on the last one, page 18, I can see some walls. Can we maybe compare with what you mean? Let us start with page 18. This is 0468-7815. There are four photos and the photo in the upright corner shows some of these walls. Would those be walls like you mean, then, as you mean them? Or are they less typical ones?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if this is indeed Skabrnja. I can only tell that it's a Croat village or settlement because I see the flag there, but I don't -- no, I'm not familiar with any of the homes in Skabrnja, to be able to tell you that this is indeed what we are talking about. If this is a photograph taken during wartime at all, there is a multitude of people here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. This is taken later probably. But maybe you didn't -- I didn't express myself clearly. I wanted to ask if it's this kind of wall you are speaking of, and maybe we can go to page 8, which is then with the last digits 7805. There is also -- there is one of these walls which look a little more sturdy and actually also taller, higher. Is this the kind of walls you are speaking of?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is the foundation of the house here. As far as I can see, this is the foundation of the house, the cellar, and the house is made of brickwork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Breeze blocks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's go back to 7815. Now, if you look at that photograph of the home where there is a flag flying, now, we understand that you don't know the village of Skabrnja, you didn't live there, you can't say whether this is Skabrnja or not. However, we have heard evidence through which these photographs were tendered and we were told that this is Skabrnja. Now, listen to the question. The question doesn't ask you whether you know this to be Skabrnja. The question is: The type of wall that you see on the perimeter of the home shown on the photograph with the flag, is that the type of wall that you remember seeing JNA soldiers taking cover behind?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. What kind of wall, then, if not this type, would that have been? Would there have been any other types of walls apart from fence walls like these on the perimeter of the yard?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are other types of walls, and they existed at the time. I don't know what Skabrnja looks like now. I know that those were stone walls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You testified also, ma'am, that people were in cellars with combatants, and that every able-bodied man was armed. My question to you is: Is it your evidence that the people were killed because they were fighting the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting. There was a war on. These were clashes between the JNA, the official army of a country that existed, and the paramilitary formations of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. So they were not killed in cross-fire, as you also testified, they were killed because they were fighting. Is that your testimony? You told us two versions.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give you two versions. Of course, people get killed when there is fighting. People don't shoot at each other with bread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know that. Let me remind you -- let me remind you of your testimony. You did say that people were in cellars with combatants and every able-bodied man was armed and you were suggesting then that because they were armed that they were in civilian clothes didn't matter, they were combatants, therefore they had to be shot at. But at some other stage you also said people were killed in cross-fire. Now, when you say people were killed in cross-fire, I understand you, and tell me if I'm wrong in my understanding, I understand you to say that they are killed by mistake, they are not combatants, but they just happened to be at the wrong place at the wrong time, hence they get shot when they shouldn't have been. Is that -- is that understanding a correct interpretation of what you meant by being shot in cross-fire?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the civilians I saw on the road, and I'm sorry that those lives were lost. They happened to find themselves in cross-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not the people in the cellars. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go down into the cellars. I don't know what was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. That ends my questions. Any questions arising from the Bench's questions, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence doesn't have any more questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just, I hope, one brief question. Further cross-examination by Mr. Black:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you were asked yesterday by His Honour Judge Hoepfel about who was in command of the JNA forces for the Skabrnja operation on the 18th and 19th of November 1991. Is it correct that the -- you mentioned Lieutenant Stefanovic, but do you know if it's correct that Lieutenant-Colonel Momcilo Bogunovic was actually higher than that, he was the person in overall command of the operation? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was the commander. I know Bogunovic and his family. He was killed, may he rest in peace. I don't know whether he was in command at the time or, in fact, who Stefanovic was subordinated to. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No further questions, urges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. Ma'am, this brings us to the end of your testimony. We want to thank you very much on behalf of the Trial Chamber for coming and taking time from your busy schedule to come and testify. Thank you very much. You are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for allowing me to tell the truth here before the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, before we call the next witness, there is just one or two housekeeping matters that the Chamber would like to raise. The first one is once again about time and about the expeditiousness of the proceedings. And in the interests of that, the Trial Chamber would like to give some kind of warning to the parties by way of addressing itself to the Defence with a reminder. The Trial Chamber has previously decided that the Defence case shall conclude on the 20th of November 2006. The Trial Chamber wants to remind the Defence that this is three weeks from today and the Trial Chamber advises the Defence to spend the remaining time wisely and to focus on areas which are relevant under the Statute and the Rules to the charges raised against the accused in the indictment. In general, the Trial Chamber considers that sufficient evidence has been led on the following topics for it to be able to come to a finding. And the Trial Chamber notes also that the Defence has led evidence through several witnesses regarding events which have taken place before 1991 and how these events influenced the Serb population in the 1990s. The Trial Chamber advises the Defence to refrain from leading evidence on topics concerning the time period before 1991 and other matters which are not a defence against the charges raised. In particular, such pre-indictment period topics are: World War II and the Ustashas, the lead-up to and the dissolution of Yugoslavia, HDZ actions and rallies and the chequer-board symbols, Croatian inflammatory media, referenda, multi-party elections, and the formation of the SDS, dismissal of Serbs from jobs, illegal arming of Croats, the ZNG and General Spegelj, barricades and the meeting at Srb. There were many others, other items will be items and I'm sure the parties are aware of this, the agreed facts, we have a filing here of the agreed facts. I think it is not necessary to canvass any evidence on those agreed facts because they are agreed. And some other evidence of a cumulative nature must also be avoided. Furthermore, the Defence should seriously consider the evidence already on the record so as not to lead any further cumulative evidence, as I've indicated, and in this vein the Defence is remind not to lead evidence on matters which are covered, as I've said, by the agreed facts. Lastly, the Trial Chamber reminds the Defence of the guidelines on the presentation of evidence and the conduct of counsel in court, wherein the Trial Chamber stressed that this Tribunal does not recognise tu quoque as a valid defence. As a consequence, the Defence must be mindful of the evidence it leads concerning the topics on Croatia -- Croat behaviour and atrocities committed against Serbs, the Vance Plan and breaches thereof by the Croats, such as Maslenica and the Medak and Operation Storm as well as both the Z-4 process and the Z-4 plan, except where they relate directly to the views, actions, or conduct of the accused on these issues. I hope that's taken. That brings me to the end of the two housekeeping matters. I don't know -- I beg your pardon. That was the one. I've got to come to the next one. I beg your pardon. For the next one, if we could move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to raise one query, I suppose with respect to the first housekeeping matter that was raised, and that is that the next witness is testifying via 92 ter, and the statement contains a number of paragraphs which address issues which Your Honours have just said need not be addressed, and specifically, for example, paragraphs 1 through 12, right off the bat I can see that those address issues. Now, I had intended in my cross-examination to address those issues because the rules kind of require us to do that, to put our case to the witness and so forth. I'm happy not to do that. I'm happy to just cross that part off my cross-examination so long as it's agreed that we will not be, in this case, penalised by that rule and that it will be understood that by doing that we are not accepting what the witness says in those paragraphs but that we have put our case to this Trial Chamber and to witnesses previously with respect to those issues, that is understood and there is no need to do so again with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The guidelines you gave us, in my view, apply to the upcoming witnesses. The witness who is about to be called has his 92 ter statement and I believe that the Prosecutor is entitled to put questions to the witness on all the points contained in the statement, even if they refer to the topics contained in your warning, because at the time we were drafting the statement we didn't have your warning before us and we proceeded according to our best judgement. I believe that my learned friend should be entitled to put questions on these matters. Otherwise, the Defence might be prejudiced in a way. I believe that under the rules, we cannot proceed other than by allowing the Prosecution to put questions on those matters and as for the witnesses coming after the next one, we will, of course, adhere to the Bench's guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, thank you for the point you are making. I think the Bench is aware of all the issues that the Prosecution has disputed, that coming from the Defence side, in relation to the matters that were mentioned in the guidelines. And I want to believe that on the basis of the guidelines that the Bench has just given, if the Prosecution does not cross-examine on those issues, and the Prosecution has also placed it on record as they have just done, that their omission to do so does not amount to an admission of those issues. I would imagine that that's sufficient to cover that point. They don't need to cross-examine on them. They can go ahead and cross-examine on the acts and conduct of the accused and the Bench will treat their silence in the same way as it will treat how it has thus far dealt with the issues referred to. So I do not think that the Defence will be prejudiced in any form. The Chamber understands that that is the stand of the Defence, in so far as those first 12 paragraphs are concerned, and we also know the stand of the Prosecution that they dispute that. I don't think it will be necessary for any cross-examination on those. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic? And let us not belabour this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall not, Your Honour. I am quite mindful of the time constraints. I do -- I'm afraid that we will come across the following point of law. What sort of weight should be given to the 12 paragraphs of the statement if the Prosecutor was not able to cross-examine the witness on these points? In addition to that, this is a very important Defence witness. We would probably have prepared his statement and examination in quite a different way. We would have perhaps sought leave to put certain questions to him in examination-in-chief. My submission is that we should deal with this witness as we have done so far and for the future witnesses, the Defence will observe the Bench's guidelines. The questions arising from the 12 paragraphs of the statement of this witness will be not dealt with, and the Trial Chamber will not be able to evaluate the witness's statement with regard to these facts, and these facts are contained in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I think the Trial Chamber is fully aware of that. The Trial Chamber has -- as it has indicated, it has heard sufficient information from the Defence about those topics and the Trial Chamber is appraised -- rather, apprised, of the Defence's standpoint on those topics. It's also aware of the Prosecution's standpoint on those topics. And there is nothing difficult --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, for interrupting you. I accept your position. I accept the Bench's position. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not wish to belabour the point any further. And that -- hence my interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I guess the next witness we are going to need more time to get him in, so it will probably be advisable to take our break now and come back at the normal time, because the technicians are going to need more time to get him organised. Court adjourned. Come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may be seated, sir. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: First I'd like to inform you with the fact that the Chamber has attributed to you a pseudonym for your protection. Your image and voice are distorted which means that during the proceedings your first and family name are not going to be mentioned. What we also will not mention are your function, your position, your business affairs, that may divulge your identity, and to this end, I'm going to present to you a document. Please read it silently, don't read it out loud, and please tell us whether this document contains your particulars, whether they are accurate, and this document also contains the pseudonym that you're going to be referred to with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I move that this document be led into evidence under seal as Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence under seal. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 996, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to ask the usher to distribute this statement to the Chamber, the OTP, and the interpreters, and the witness. We've prepared sufficient copies for the interpreters as well, three copies. Here you are. I think that one copy should be given to the witness so that he may confirm its veracity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at this statement in front of you, and please tell us whether this statement is that which you gave to the -- to Mr. Nikolic, investigator of the Defence, and please testify that you've read it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes. I've read it and gave that statement and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us whether you would give such a statement if you were to be examined and testify viva voce regarding these facts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes. I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move that this statement be admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The statement is admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that exhibit should be placed under seal, the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do think you are right, Mr. Whiting. May the exhibit please be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] One moment, please. All right. Before that is done, I wonder whether we could get the date when the statement was given from the witness. I don't believe that is on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can inquire, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Alex Whiting. I'm one of the prosecutors in this case. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will have to -- because of your protective measures I will refer to you either as Witness, sir, or sometimes maybe even as Witness MM-105. If we talk about any matters which could disclosure you're identity I'll ask that we go into private session but if we are in public session and you want to give an answer that you think would disclose your identity, please just tell us and we can move into private session. Do you understand? I think you nodded your head but that's not recorded in the transcript so if you could answer verbally that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: I understand. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, could -- the statement that you have in front of you, could you tell us when you gave this statement to the Defence investigator, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: I think that I gave this statement some 15 days ago but nothing material has changed in the meantime. I fully confirm the -- what I said in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you gave the statement 15 days ago, and it appears from the first page of it that you actually only signed it today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I think on every page this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I had only looked at the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But is it true that the indication is on every page that you signed the statement today? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: That is correct. And it's on every page, together with my signature and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'm not -- for reasons that the Trial Chamber and the Defence counsel understand, I will not ask you about every paragraph of this statement. I'm only going to ask you about certain specific paragraphs. But before I do that, I just want to ask you a couple of questions to kind of situate your testimony. It's true, isn't it, that your statement is primarily about Okucani, which is situated in an area known as Western Slavonia, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: It is not correct. It refers to Okucani as the local municipality, but that affects through the whole territory of RSK, Croatia, and the whole Yugoslavia. You had to consider the whole context to go from the general to the particular, from the general to the local.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But you agree with me that Okucani is in Western Slavonia, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just so we are clear, the Serbian Autonomous District of Western Slavonia, which is sometimes referred to as the SAO Western Slavonia, was established on the 12th of August 1991, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the president of that entity, when it was established, was Veljko Dzakula, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And during 1991, during the remainder of 1991, from that date, August 12th, 1991, until actually until February of 1992, the SAO Western Slavonia was a separate entity from the SAO Krajina, correct? It was completely a separate entity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: That is correct. It was separated and it encompassed the area of Western Slavonia in the Serbian historical and ethnical boundaries but the programme [indiscernible] our agenda was complementary with the areas of Krajina, Banija, Kordun, Lika, et cetera, with the capital in Knin. Of course, we had the same problems facing us and we could not have different opinions about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But just so we are clear, the individuals who were in power in the SAO Krajina had no authority in the SAO Western Slavonia during 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: In part, because the municipality of Pakrac, which was joined by Okucani and other municipalities wishing to do so, and in Daruvar, parts of Daruvar municipality, those municipalities accepted the entry into the Serbian Krajina, not all of them. Pakrac and Daruvar, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They did that earlier in 1991 but when the SAO Western Slavonia was created in August of 1991, they joined the SAO Western Slavonia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just so we are clear, it was not actually until the 26th of February 1992 that the SAO Western Slavonia joined together with the SAO Krajina and also the SAO Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem to form what then became the RSK or the Republika Srpska Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Correct in part, because Okucani and Pakrac took part on the constituent assembly on the 19th of December 1991, when the Republic of Serbian Krajina was established in Knin. They sent their delegates and this is how they took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But other than that little clarification, what I said is correct about the date when the SAO Western Slavonia joined together with the SAO Krajina, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes. The 26th of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to -- in paragraph 13 of your statement, and you'll see I've skipped a number of paragraphs but moving to paragraph 13 of your statement, you say that Croatia pushed the Serbs into separatism. But isn't it true, sir, that in 1991, the Croatian side offered forms of autonomy to the Serb side in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Sincerely, nothing was offered apart from the establishment of a body which was supposed to prepare the background materials to define some sort of an autonomy but I do believe that this was just a foil to improve the image towards the international community, but there was nothing material in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please, Your Honour? I'm sorry to keep doing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, we are talking about now about a meeting that occurred around the 12th of March 1991, between Tudjman and some Serb leaders in Croatia. Isn't it a fact that Tudjman promised autonomy in education, culture and information to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: There was talk about that, on certain modalities of autonomy, but both sides discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to press this a little bit. Isn't it true that actually he promised autonomy in those areas? Not that it was just discussed but that he promised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. It really will be helpful if you could listen to my question and only answer my question. Okay? Because here in your last answer you've really strayed quite far from what my question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of the usher I'd like to put before the witness a document and I have copies for everybody, including the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Milovancevic, are we in private or open session? We are in open session. Can we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right but just to be clear, paragraph 16 of the statement for here, not the OTP statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that Serbs took control in areas where they were the majority as early as August of 1990 and after that in through 1991, correct? You'd agree with me about that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: They did, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, that's fine. Then in -- also in 1990 and into 1991, the Serbs in the majority Serb areas started to create political structures, in June of 1990, for example, the association of Northern Dalmatia and Lika was created. And then in December of 1990, the SAO Krajina was established. So they started to create political structures in those Serb areas, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you say in your statement here in paragraph 16 that they had -- or that they tried to link up the territories where they were the majority. Now, in other words, they had to link up Serb territories that were separated by areas where Croats were the majority, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes. To link up those Serb territories that can be smoothly linked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the goal was to create a contiguous state of Serb territories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: I don't think I ever mentioned the word "state." We are speaking of territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the goal, what I'm putting to you is that the goal of linking up these territories was to create a contiguous territory where Serbs were the majority and where they would have their political structures and where they would have ultimately their own state, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: There was no mention of the state. This was a reaction to the Croatian policies which excommunicated the Serbs from the Croatian society.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's put aside the concept of a state for a moment and let's put aside the reason that this may have been done. All I'm trying to establish with you is that you would agree with me that the goal was to connect together these Serb territories into a contiguous territory where -- where they could have their political structures as they were being formed in 1990 and 1991, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: This was a rational solution. Any other solution would have ended up in anarchy and absence of rule of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Should that be taken as a yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is -- well, had these territories not been linked up, how would key have been able to have vital institutions? Because Croatia had discontinued the payment of salaries to public agencies, the payment of pensions to the pensioners, Serbs found themselves in a ghetto where they had to interconnect themselves to function at the local level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We understand all that. If we go on like this we may not finish. My question was very simple. Shall we accept that first answer as a yes to the question that was put to you? The question that was put to you required either a yes or a no, and you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. But these are not exact sciences and where my answer would be yes or no. It can't be given a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that some questions may not be given a yes or no answer but there is one of those few that can. The question was simply that you would agree with the Prosecutor that the goal was to connect together these Serb territories into a contiguous territory where they were -- where they could have their political structures as they were being formed in 1990 and 1991. Now, either that is correct or it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. To be linked up with a view to meeting the needs of the population inhabiting the areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The purpose is something else, but -- why these had to be put together, these territories, is something else, but before they could be put -- before you could accept that, you could achieve that purpose, these territories had to be put together, like indeed you finally got the SAO Krajina, the SAO Western Slavonia, and the others, into the RSK. That was the natural progression. Is that correct? And I think it's not difficult to say whether it was or was not correct. Whether it is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's correct, as I said in order to organise life in the area that was the precondition for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to talk about the reason that it was done because you have insisted in your answers again and again and you say to be fair in your statement that it was a defensive action by the Serbs, but, sir, are you aware that in May of 1991, Milan Babic told the assembly in the SAO Krajina -- and maybe you won't be aware of this because it was in the Krajina -- that the Krajina belonged ethnically and historically with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a reference to Exhibit 955, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware that he told the assembly that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, and it is not my intention to be the censor of his statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware that Milan Babic, as the president of the SAO Krajina, held that view, that joining together the Krajina with its majority-Serb area with Serbia was a historically determined act?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: I do know that this was his idea, and in some ways an intention on his part, which dictated some of his moves. However, I cannot comment on his thoughts. The Serbian people found it hard to get reconciled with the break-up of Yugoslavia, and that was why certain steps were taken because the Serbian people did not live in one state. They were scattered throughout the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look -- go to paragraph 21 of your statement here, that's been admitted into evidence here, and do you have that in front of you? And I just want to make sure you're looking at the correct statement. It's the one that you signed --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: This latest statement? Not the one given to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's right, the latest one, the one signed today. And you say in that statement, and I'm going to read it out because I want to compare it to something you said earlier, you say that, "On the 14th or 15th of August, the Croatian police entered Okucani with personnel carriers and a large number of vehicles. Via megaphone, they asked the people to surrender their weapons, called on them to be loyal to the Croatian state and authorities, and as far as I remember, there was shooting near the house of Nikola Metijevic [phoen] who was bed ridden. The provocation and demonstration of force caused the reaction on the Serbian side and the Serbs fired on a personnel carrier from a rocket launcher but the shell missed its target and hit a Serbian house." Now, if you wouldn't mind, could we look, please, at how you described this same incident in your statement to the OTP? And it's paragraph 18 of that statement, and if we could start from the fourth sentence, which starts, "The very first conflict happened on the 15th of August because on the 14th of August, the Croats came to Okucani in the APCs, vehicles, the Croatian police went in the house of Milenko Miljevic, who was an electrician, and searched the house for weapons. At that time Croatia was not internationally recognised and for the Serbs these operations were considered illegal and abuses. The Croatian police were supposed to operate in accordance with the legislation in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. From the legal point of view, the Croatian police were abusing and harassing the Serbian population." Now, these two versions, I put to you, of what happened on August 14th, the one that is in your statement is in evidence here today and the one that you gave to the OTP are quite different. Can you tell us which one is true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you that the accounts are different. It is only that Milenko Miljevic was mentioned here. I mentioned the APC. The megaphone over which persons were called upon to surrender weapons. Well, did you really expect the Serbs to oppose the Croatian paramilitary forces which had been illegally arming themselves with slings?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's try to be a little precise about the differences between these two statements. In your statement you give here today, it's very broadly put that the Croatian police came in and via megaphone asked everybody to surrender their weapons, and called on them to be loyal, and there was shooting and that this was a provocation and demonstration of force but in the OTP statement, what you say is that the Croatian police came in for a very specific purpose, to search a house for weapons and that this was considered offensive because the Croatia was not internationally recognised. And that this was -- this search for weapons was considered abusive. So those are really two very different things. Now, can you tell us which account, what really happened? Was it the account, this broad account that you have given in your statement to the Court or was it this more specific event that you gave in your OTP statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: These are not two different things. I wouldn't agree with you. We were maintaining peace in the area of Okucani in agreement with the Nova Gradiska authorities. Our verbal agreement meant that they should not be sending members of the Croatian police who had new insignia to Okucani because this caused revolt on the part of the Serbs. However, there came this order from Zagreb that they should enter the area and this provoked the conflict. I believe that this was a move on the part of the Croatian authorities which was rash because that was the area where at one time 90 per cent Serbs lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, can you tell me where in the OTP account you say that they -- the Croat authorities via megaphone asked the people to surrender their weapons? Can you show me where that is said in the OTP statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: It doesn't say that. However, regardless of that, it's a point of fact, and it doesn't matter in it's contained here or there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it's kind of an important fact, isn't it? Why is that left out of your account that you gave to the OTP? Isn't that in fact -- wouldn't that be the most important fact about this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: I don't think so. The important thing is that there was a show of force, which expressed itself in the form of APCs, calls upon the surrendering of weapons, whether a megaphone is mentioned or not is not something that would determine the fate of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, did that really happen? Was there really a call for surrender of weapons or was it, as you describe in your OTP statement, simply an operation to do a specific search for weapons at a particular house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Well, no. There wasn't a specific house, but the person involved had hunting rifles. He was a hunter. That's why. This was just a show of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What you describe as a show of force was that the Croatian authorities went to this house of Milenko Miljevic, who was an electrician, and searched his house for weapons. That's what was a show of force, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes. But this did not involve only one house. His father, Nikola, lay in bed. He was bed ridden and the person wasn't at home. Miroslav Zupancic an HDZ MP, who was a sculptor, I think, he was on the APC and together with another person he called on the local population to be loyal to the Croatian authorities. I was there and I saw that. It was just a show of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that last little part that you've provided to us, was that -- that's not in your OTP statement, is it? You don't talk about that in your OTP statement, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if I were to detail everything, I would end up writing a novel longer -- a novel that would be longer than "War and Peace" by Tolstoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I appreciate the sense of humour as much as anybody but the truth is that your statement that's in evidence in this court is only nine pages, far short of War and Peace, isn't that true, sir? And you found room in this statement to talk about the megaphone and the surrendering of weapons and so forth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes. Nine pages. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is it true, what you say in paragraph 19 of your OTP statement, that on the 15th of August 1991, 50 young Serbs tried to liberate Okucani, and there was an exchange of fire with the ZNG and the Croatian police? Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt? Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, could we look at -- well, after this event occurred in Okucani and the clash occurred there in the middle of August of 1991, the Presidency of the SFRY intervened; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could look at paragraph 23 of your -- what I'll call your trial statement, we'll call the statement you signed today your trial statement and your other statement your OTP statement, just so we can keep them straight and if you could look at paragraph 23 of your trial statement, you say that the Presidency delegation took the view that blame was to be equally apportioned to two sides but that you objected because the Croats had come to a purely Serb area and flexed their muscles. So is it your view, sir, that where Serbs were in the majority, Serbs should have been left alone and the Croat authorities should have stayed away? Is that your view of what -- how things should have been done in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: It is. This is what I think. Croatian forces should not have come to the area of Okucani because it was calm. There was no reason for the arrival of Croatian police forces. Nothing had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well wait a minute. That's a different statement than what's why in your trial statement of paragraph 23. You say we objected because Croats had come to a purely Serbian area and flexed their muscles. And that's what you objected to, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: That is correct because there was no need for them to come into Okucani. It was tantamount to intimidation, harassment of the population, spreading fear, doubt. Had anything in the form of an incident happened, then we would have invited them. We had agreement with Nova Gradiska, an oral agreement, for Serb policemen to be sent into Okucani because some Serb policemen still worked in Nova Gradiska police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's explore that a little bit. You say there was no reason but from your own account about there event of why the Croatian authorities came to Okucani, it was in order to search for weapons. That is a legitimate reason for the police authorities to act, correct? So they in fact did have a reason to come, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: No. They did not have any reason to come in that way, because it was a public secret that at the same time both sides had already been armed. But it could -- could have transpired that a balance of fear could have been created to avoid the use of weapons. The arrival of the Croatian police there was with the sole aim of provoking a conflict and that would lead to what which really happened later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So -- let me just see if I understand you. Really, aren't you saying that the Croat authorities should have just left the Serbs alone, even if they had weapons, they should have just left them alone, in the Serb-majority areas? Isn't that really what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes. They should have -- should not have -- they should have left them alone and when preconditions had been created for negotiations, some compromise could have been reached and it's better to negotiate for 100 days rather than to fight a war for a single day, but Croatian Democratic Union had promised Croatia, Croatia to Croatians. Serbs were no longer constituent people and they lost Croatia as soon as they no longer were a constituent nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, again, please just focus on my questions. You fully answered that question when you said the word "yes." Okay? And all of the rest of it really was not necessary. Now, did you have the same view of Serb authorities going into majority-Croat areas? Did you think that the Serb authorities should have stayed out of the Croat areas and just left them alone in the same way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: I always had a clear and unambiguous position. I do not apply double standards. Only one standard, one principle, and it applies to both Croatians, Serbs, Czechs, Slovakians, Hungarians, this is what I required [as interpreted] through my education and my democratic outlook on the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes, you had the same view of Serb authorities going into majority-Croat areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 23, you explain -- of your trial statement, you explain that a buffer zone was created by the JNA, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then you say, in paragraph 24, that General Raseta flew by helicopter from Zagreb to Okucani and that his helicopter was shot at; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not the same event. General Raseta came with Henri Wijnaendts from the European Community. He came in his company to negotiate. Those two events do not have anything in common.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, but what I was focused at is that you say his helicopter was shot at and you say further that it was shot at by members of the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: This is correct, from Gornji Bogicevci at that time Croatian police, and the National Guards Corps held the Croatian village of Gornji Bogicevci near Okucani and this is from where the helicopter was fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then you say, as a result of this, there was an offensive launched by the Okucani Territorial Defence and part of the Banja Luka Corps of the JNA, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So let me just get clear on this. The helicopter is fired at and this then results in an offensive by the Territorial Defence and the JNA, which resulted in the Croat forces withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: You draw an incorrect conclusion from incorrect premises. We are talking about the Territorial Defence of Okucani, who set out to liberate Okucani from Croatian police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what was the incorrect premise and what was the incorrect conclusion. I was just tracking what you say in your statement. Isn't it -- didn't you just agree with me that the helicopter was fired at and, as a result of that, an offensive was launched by the Territorial Defence and the JNA? And that as a result of that offensive, the Croatian forces withdrew? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, by no means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness just said the TO in his answer at line 16 -- wait a minute. At line 12. Wait a minute. What am I looking at? Yes, line 19. We are talking about the Territorial Defence of Okucani who set out to liberate Okucani from Croatian police. He seems to exclude the JNA. And your question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no JNA, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let me explore that. Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciates that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to know what the Banja Luka Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's going to be my next question, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you -- let's look at paragraph 25 of your trial statement. You say -- before we do, let me just get clear on one thing. The reason the offensive occurred, we will talk about who participated in the offensive but the reason the offensive occurred was because the helicopter was fired at; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: It has no connection with that, this helicopter. You are adamant in not understanding what I'm saying to you. Why would an attack ensue from firing at the helicopter carrying General Raseta and Henri Wijnaendts? No. There was a group of young TO from Okucani in the area of the Psunj mountain and they exercised their right to liberate their own hometowns and attacked them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour, if you -- if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: First, I'm sorry if I misunderstood you, sir, but you had agreed with me earlier that the attack occurred as a result of the attack on the helicopter, but now you've clarified your answer and if we could just be clear now, the -- you say that the attack was by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I apologise. An objection, Your Honour. I don't know whether it was translated verbatim but I understand the witness's language. This was what he said: The offensive at Okucani had nothing to do with the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has nothing to do with the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true, but that's not what Mr. Whiting was talking about. Mr. Whiting was talking about the shooting at the helicopter being a cause for the offensive, a reason for the offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I may, what I was referring to is at page 52, line 12, where I said, my question was, "and then you say as a result of this there was an offensive launched by the Okucani Territorial Defence and part of the Banja Luka Corps of the JNA, correct?" The answer was: "That's correct."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's line 12 of page 52. So I -- but I appreciate that he now says that that it was not the cause for the attack or what's that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me just see if I can press --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: These are two incompatible events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So let's -- what was the reason for the attack by the TO of Okucani on the Croatian police? What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: The reason was a patriotic one and a heroic one because parents, sisters, brothers, of the TO of Okucani who had withdrawn and retreated to Psunj area, they were under lock and key of the Croatian force, they thought it their democratic right to liberate their own home town; in my opinion, that's a basic right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But what about the JNA buffer zone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: The JNA had not arrived. This was conflict of the ones and the others. Then Varazdin Corps of the JNA, a tank unit, arrived to create a buffer zone before the -- between the two sides. What you are referring to occurred after the arrival of a delegation of the assembly of Yugoslavia, Presidency of Yugoslavia, and the General Staff of Yugoslavia. And as a consequence of that conflict, they were sent to come here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please, we are going to have to take a break in a moment but let me just see if I can get the sequence of events right. Didn't the buffer zone -- wasn't the -- didn't the JNA establish the buffer zone and then after that, the -- there was the shooting of the helicopter and then after that, there was the attack, the offensive, by the Okucani Territorial Defence? Just the sequence of events occurred in that order, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-105
utterances.text: No, no. This is the sequence: First, show of force on the part of the Croatian police. Second, attack by the Territorial Defence of Okucani on the Croatian police to push them away from Okucani and villages around Okucani. They withdrew two days after, well, after first skirmishes, really. Then, third, delegations of the assembly Presidency and General Staff of Yugoslavia coming here and 15, 20 days ago, later, helicopter carrying General Raseta and Henri Wijnaendts was fired at, and they came here to discuss modalities of organising the life in the areas of Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well we are going to have to look a little more carefully at your statement then. If we could take the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Court is going to take a short break. We'll come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting. We are reaching the halfway mark in 15 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The halfway mark of what, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of the witness's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that was a time that was set not by us or not by any -- that was just a time that was arbitrarily set by the Defence and I'm going to need a lot more time and I'm also advised, and I don't think Mr. Milovancevic will mind if I say this, that I don't think the next witness is available until Friday and so I think there will be plenty of time to cross-examine the witness. But we never agreed to that time limit and I don't think the time limit was the -- I don't think the time limit was appropriate for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But are you saying you're not bound by it now because you never agreed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, what I'm saying -- I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
